title: Type 1 Diabetes
about: The body makes no insulin and daily insulin injections are needed for life, matched to food and activity.
managementGoals: Take insulin exactly as prescribed — the type, dose and timing are matched to meals
Check blood glucose as taught, and keep a written record to bring to clinic
Count carbohydrates and eat regular, balanced meals — no skipped meals after insulin
Learn personal low-sugar warning signs and always carry fast sugar (glucose sweets, cold drink, sugar sachets)
Clinic reviews: HbA1c about every three to six months, plus eyes, feet, kidneys and blood pressure yearly
Sick-day plan: illness raises sugar — never stop insulin when sick, test more often, and know when to seek help
adherenceTips: Anchor insulin doses to a daily routine — breakfast, supper — so a dose is never silently missed
Keep one spare insulin pen or vial and needles at home; insulin in use can stay at room temperature for a month, spare insulin belongs in the fridge
Rotate injection sites to avoid lumps that make insulin absorb unpredictably
Tell school and work what to do for a low-sugar emergency, and where the fast sugar is kept
whenToSeekUrgentCare: Vomiting and unable to keep fluids down, with a high sugar reading
Deep fast breathing, fruity-smelling breath, drowsiness or confusion (diabetic ketoacidosis — emergency)
A low-sugar episode that does not recover after two rounds of fast sugar, or a convulsion
A foot wound, blister or sore that is not healing, however small

source.authority: SA NDoH diabetes guidelines / ISPAD / WHO

title: Type 2 Diabetes
about: The most common form of diabetes in South Africa — insulin resistance treated with tablets, sometimes insulin, and always with food, movement and weight control.
managementGoals: Take tablets every day at the same time, with food if metformin upsets the stomach
HbA1c (the three-month sugar average) usually aimed below 7% — individualised with the clinician
Blood pressure below 140/90 (often below 130/80 where kidneys are involved) — diabetes and blood pressure damage the same organs together
Feet: look at both feet every day, wash and dry between the toes, closed shoes that fit, never barefoot
Eyes: a retina check every year — diabetes blinds quietly
Healthy plate: half vegetables, a quarter starch, a quarter protein; water instead of sweet drinks; walk 30 minutes most days
Yearly clinic review of kidneys (urine and blood tests) and cholesterol
adherenceTips: Chronic medicine collection through the clinic's fast queue or CCMDD pick-up points so the tablets never run out
Link tablet-taking to a fixed daily event — brushing teeth, breakfast — and use a seven-day pill box
Collect the next supply in the final week of the current one, never the day it finishes
Keep clinic appointments even when feeling well — type 2 diabetes damages silently for years before it hurts
whenToSeekUrgentCare: Drowsiness, deep breathing, fruity breath, or sugar readings staying very high with vomiting
Any foot wound, corn or blister that is discoloured, weeping or not healing — same week, not same month
Chest pain, one-sided weakness or sudden speech trouble (diabetes raises heart and stroke risk sharply)
Low-sugar episodes (shaking, sweating, confusion) — treat with sugar and adjust treatment at the clinic afterwards

title: Hypertension
about: Blood pressure that stays at or above 140/90 — usually silent, and the leading driver of stroke, heart failure and kidney failure in South Africa.
managementGoals: Blood pressure below 140/90 for most people, and often below 130/80 where diabetes or kidney disease is present
Medicine every single day — blood pressure tablets work only while they are in the body; feeling well means they are working, not that they can stop
Salt: less than one level teaspoon (5g) a day, including stock cubes, soup powders, processed meats and salty snacks
Weight, movement and alcohol: even 5kg of weight loss lowers pressure; 30 minutes of walking most days; alcohol in moderation or not at all
No smoking — each cigarette pushes the pressure up and hardens the arteries
Yearly checks: urine for protein, glucose, cholesterol and eyes
adherenceTips: Never stop tablets because the reading is normal — normal is the tablets
Do not stop when side effects appear — a persistent cough or ankle swelling has an alternative medicine; tell the clinic rather than enduring or quitting
Take water tablets in the morning so sleep is not broken
Home readings help: sit five minutes first, arm supported at heart level, two readings, same time daily — bring the written record to clinic
whenToSeekUrgentCare: Reading above 180/120 with headache, chest pain, vision change, breathlessness or weakness — hypertensive emergency
Sudden weakness, facial droop or speech trouble — call 10177 (stroke)
Chest pressure lasting more than a few minutes, with sweating or nausea
Breathlessness lying flat, or waking gasping with swollen ankles

title: HIV on Antiretroviral Treatment
about: HIV is a lifelong condition treated with one tablet a day (usually the TLD combination), which keeps the virus suppressed and lets a normal healthy life and lifespan be expected.
managementGoals: One tablet, once a day, at the same time — viral suppression is the goal and it depends almost entirely on not missing doses
Viral load blood test about every six months: under 50 copies means undetectable — and undetectable means the virus cannot be passed on through sex
CD4 count and TB screening at intervals the clinic sets; TB is the most common serious illness alongside HIV in South Africa
Annual checks of kidney function (tenofovir), weight, blood pressure and, for women, cervical screening
Condoms and partner testing; treatment is for life even when the viral load is undetectable
adherenceTips: Tie the dose to something done daily without fail — a meal, a radio show, bedtime — and keep a week's supply in a place seen every day
A missed dose is taken when remembered, unless it is nearly time for the next dose — then skip the missed one; never take a double dose
Separate the tablet from antacids, iron and calcium supplements by at least two hours
Use CCMDD pick-up points for collection so queues never become a reason to run out
Adherence clubs and support groups help — ask the clinic what exists in the area
Tell the clinic before starting any traditional or herbal remedies — some reduce ART levels
whenToSeekUrgentCare: A new or worsening rash, especially with blisters, mouth ulcers or fever
Rapid weight loss, night sweats or a cough beyond two weeks (possible TB)
Yellow eyes, severe stomach pain with vomiting, or a fever with confusion
Trouble keeping tablets down for more than a day

title: Tuberculosis Treatment
about: Drug-sensitive TB is cured by six months of daily tablets — two months of four medicines (RHZE), then four months of two — taken exactly as prescribed.
managementGoals: Finish all six months — feeling better after a few weeks is expected, and stopping then is what creates drug resistance
Take the tablets on an empty stomach with water, before breakfast, as the clinic teaches
Sputum tests at two months and at the end of treatment confirm the cure
Good food and rest support recovery; the clinic arranges nutrition support where needed
Household contacts, especially children and people living with HIV, are screened and offered preventive therapy
adherenceTips: Treatment is taken in front of a treatment supporter in the SA programme — agree on a supporter whose daily routine fits
Orange-red urine, sweat and tears are normal and expected on rifampicin
Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) is usually given alongside to protect the nerves
Keep every clinic date — tracing teams follow up missed doses because unfinished treatment is how MDR-TB is born
whenToSeekUrgentCare: Yellow eyes, dark urine, severe nausea or upper tummy pain (liver reaction — same day)
Vision changes or difficulty distinguishing colours (ethambutol — same day)
Rash, itching that spreads, or fever with a rash
Coughing blood, worsening breathlessness, drenching night sweats returning

title: Drug-Resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB)
about: TB that the standard medicines cannot cure — treatment is longer, uses different medicines, and is coordinated by specialist TB units, but newer all-tablet regimens have made cure far more achievable than in the past.
managementGoals: Complete the full course — modern regimens are typically about six months for suitable patients, longer where the doctors advise
Regular reviews and tests: sputum cultures, hearing and vision checks where the regimen requires, and blood tests
Household screening of all contacts, with children evaluated for preventive treatment
Treatment is free in the public sector, including transport support in many districts — ask the TB unit what is available
adherenceTips: Every single dose matters more than in ordinary TB — resistance deepens with each missed dose
Set phone alarms for each dosing time and use a diary; many regimens have tablets at different times of day
Tell the team about every other medicine, supplement and traditional remedy — interactions are common in these regimens
Depression and fatigue are common companions of long treatment — say so at the visit; it is treatable and it protects the course
whenToSeekUrgentCare: Rash, hearing change, ringing in the ears, or vision change — same day
Yellow eyes, severe tingling or burning feet, or low mood with thoughts of self-harm — same day
Coughing blood or worsening breathlessness
A fever that arrives while on treatment

source.authority: SA NDoH DR-TB guidelines / WHO consolidated DR-TB guidance

title: Asthma
about: Reversible airway inflammation — controlled by a daily preventer inhaler, with a reliever kept for attacks.
managementGoals: Take the preventer inhaler every day, even when breathing is completely well — it prevents the attacks, it does not treat them
Use the reliever only when needed: needing it more than twice a week, or at night, means the preventer plan needs review
Know and avoid triggers: smoke (including indoor paraffin and wood smoke), pollens, dust, strong smells, colds
Have a written action plan from the clinic: what to do when symptoms rise, when to increase the preventer, when to get help
Annual flu vaccine, free at clinics for people with asthma
Check inhaler technique at every clinic visit — most inhalers are wasted by poor technique, and a spacer improves delivery for children and in attacks
adherenceTips: Keep the preventer beside the toothbrush — twice-daily doses attach to brushing teeth
Rinse and spit after every preventer dose to prevent thrush
Do not let the reliever run out: count doses remaining and refill before the last twenty puffs
Discard old inhalers that pass their date — an empty inhaler in a crisis is a recognised danger
whenToSeekUrgentCare: Reliever not helping, or wearing off within four hours
Cannot finish a sentence in one breath, sitting hunched forward, lips or tongue bluish
Attacks at night that wake the person, or a peak flow in the red zone of the action plan
Any child with asthma who cannot talk, play or feed — call 10177

title: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)
about: Permanent narrowing of the airways, usually from years of smoking or smoke exposure — breathlessness on effort that worsens over years, with flare-ups that can be life-threatening.
managementGoals: Stop smoking — the single intervention that changes the disease's course; ask the clinic for support programmes
Inhalers exactly as prescribed, and technique checked at each visit
Pulmonary rehabilitation and regular walking within tolerance — fitness is oxygen economy
Annual flu vaccine and pneumococcal vaccination
Plan for flare-ups: know the personal warning signs (more breathless, more sputum, change in colour) and the action plan
adherenceTips: Inhalers only work with correct technique — take the inhaler to every clinic visit and show, do not describe
Never run out of the regular inhalers; keep a rescue course of tablets at home if the clinic has prescribed one
Avoid smoke-filled rooms, dust and strong chemicals; ventilate cooking fires where possible
Eat smaller frequent meals — a full stomach pushes on the lungs; keep weight healthy, neither losing nor gaining excessively
whenToSeekUrgentCare: Sudden worsening of breathlessness or confusion — emergency
Fever with more sputum that has turned green, yellow or rusty
Blue lips, swollen ankles with breathlessness, or drowsiness
Chest pain with breathlessness

source.authority: GOLD strategy / SA NDoH chronic respiratory care

title: Epilepsy
about: A tendency to recurrent seizures, controlled by daily anti-seizure medicine in most people.
managementGoals: Medicine every day at consistent times — seizure control lives or dies on steady blood levels
Regular sleep — missed sleep is the commonest seizure trigger after missed doses
Limit alcohol; avoid swimming alone, working at heights and unguarded machinery
Driving: South African licensing requires a seizure-free period on treatment before driving — follow the licensing authority's requirement and the treating doctor's advice
Clinic reviews with drug-level or other blood tests where the doctor orders them, plus bone health checks on long-term enzyme-inducing medicines
adherenceTips: Never stop tablets abruptly — withdrawal seizures can be worse than the originals; changes are made by the clinician slowly
One missed dose: take it when remembered unless the next is nearly due — never double up
Wear or carry a medical identification card or band stating epilepsy and the medicines
Teach family the first-aid basics: side, cushion, nothing in the mouth, time the seizure, and when to call 10177
whenToSeekUrgentCare: Any seizure lasting beyond five minutes, or seizures repeating without full recovery between them — call 10177
A first seizure in someone not known to have epilepsy
Seizure with injury, in water, or during pregnancy
Rash while on anti-seizure medicine — same-day care, it can be serious

title: Chronic Kidney Disease
about: Slow loss of kidney function, usually from hypertension, diabetes or HIV — often silent until late, and protected mainly by blood pressure and sugar control.
managementGoals: Blood pressure control is kidney protection: the target is often below 130/80 with the clinic's guidance
Blood sugar control in diabetes protects the kidneys as much as the eyes
Avoid ibuprofen, naproxen and similar anti-inflammatory tablets — they reduce blood flow through the kidneys; paracetamol is the safer pain choice
Avoid unverified herbal and traditional remedies without telling the clinic — some are directly toxic to kidneys
Blood and urine tests on the clinic's schedule track the decline, and dietitian advice adjusts salt, protein and potassium
Where kidney disease is advanced, planning ahead for dialysis or transplant options happens at specialist clinics
adherenceTips: Take the protective medicines (blood pressure tablets, sometimes others) even though they treat nothing a person can feel
Bring every medicine and supplement to clinic visits — the clinic can only protect kidneys from what it knows about
Avoid dehydration in hot weather and during diarrhoea — kidneys suffer first
Treat urinary infections early; recurring infections speed the decline
whenToSeekUrgentCare: Passing much less urine than usual, or none over a day
Breathlessness, swollen legs or face that is new or worsening
Confusion or unusual drowsiness
Chest pain — kidney disease and heart disease travel together

source.authority: WHO / SA NDoH renal care guidance

title: Hypothyroidism
about: An underactive thyroid treated with one daily levothyroxine tablet for life.
managementGoals: Levothyroxine once daily, on an empty stomach, 30-60 minutes before food, with water only
Blood test (TSH) on the clinic's schedule — the dose is tuned to it
Keep the same tablet brand where possible, and report pregnancy early — the dose usually rises
adherenceTips: Keep iron tablets, calcium and antacids at least four hours away from the thyroid tablet — they block its absorption
Morning routine: thyroid tablet first, kettle on, breakfast a full hour later
A missed dose is taken later the same day; do not double the next day
Feeling changes — new tiredness, feeling cold, weight change, palpitations — may mean the dose needs retuning, not that the medicine has failed
whenToSeekUrgentCare: Extreme drowsiness with cold skin and slow breathing (rare, severe underactivity — emergency)
New fast or irregular heartbeat, sweating and weight loss after a dose increase — clinic the same week
Pregnancy or planning pregnancy — same-week clinic visit for dose adjustment

source.authority: WHO / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

title: Rheumatic Heart Disease
about: Heart valve damage from untreated strep throat in childhood — South Africa carries a significant burden, and monthly penicillin injections prevent further damage.
managementGoals: Monthly (every four weeks) benzathine penicillin injection, for years — the doctor sets the duration, commonly into adulthood
Every sore throat in a person with known heart valve disease is assessed and treated — a fresh strep infection is what damages the valves further
Regular heart reviews as the clinic schedules, and dental care with antibiotics before dental procedures when advised
Family screening: siblings and children of an affected person are checked
Planning pregnancy with the heart team — valve disease changes pregnancy risk
adherenceTips: The injection date belongs on the calendar and a reminder with it; the clinic keeps the schedule — keep every appointment
Never skip because the last injection was painful — ask for a different injection site or a slower technique, but never skip
Carry a card stating the diagnosis; it changes how new clinicians treat sore throats and dental care
Report breathlessness on effort, palpitations or swelling of ankles — valve damage announces change through these
whenToSeekUrgentCare: Breathlessness at rest, or waking at night gasping
A fever that lasts days with weight loss and night sweats (possible heart valve infection — emergency)
New irregular heartbeat or fainting
Chest pain

source.authority: SA NDoH rheumatic fever and RHD guidance / WHO

title: Atrial Fibrillation and Anticoagulation
about: An irregular heart rhythm treated with blood thinners (usually warfarin in the public sector) to prevent stroke.
managementGoals: The blood-thinning tablet every single day, at the same time — its protection depends on steady levels
INR blood tests on the clinic's schedule (often monthly once stable): the result decides the dose — keep every appointment
Keep vitamin K intake steady: green vegetables are healthy and should not be avoided, just eaten consistently rather than in sudden binges
Heart rate control tablets exactly as prescribed, with the pulse checked as taught
Alcohol limits: binge drinking destabilises both the rhythm and the INR
adherenceTips: A fixed evening dose with a phone reminder; a seven-day pill box makes missed days visible
Tell every new clinician, dentist and pharmacist about the blood thinner before any procedure or new medicine
Carry a card or wear a band naming the medicine and its purpose
Keep a small written record of INR results and doses — it shortens every clinic visit
whenToSeekUrgentCare: Any fall or knock to the head, however minor — bleeding inside the skull can hide for hours
Bleeding that will not stop, blood in urine or stool, black tarry stools, coughing or vomiting blood, sudden severe bruising
New weakness, speech trouble or vision loss — call 10177 (stroke)
An irregular pulse that comes with chest pain, fainting or breathlessness

source.authority: WHO / SA NDoH cardiovascular care guidance

title: Gout — Long-Term Management
about: Recurring attacks of excruciating joint inflammation from urate crystals — long-term daily medicine dissolves the crystals and stops the attacks.
managementGoals: Daily allopurinol, started low and raised slowly by the clinician — its goal is a blood urate level, not the absence of attacks this month
Once established on allopurinol, continue it through flares unless the doctor says otherwise — stopping and starting keeps the urate level swinging, and swings cause flares
Fluids: two litres or more of water daily, more in hot weather or hard work
Cut the drivers: beer and spirits, sugary cold drinks, organ meats, large meat portions; keep to a healthy weight without crash dieting
adherenceTips: Allopurinol is taken every day, not only when a joint hurts — the attacks and the medicine work on different clocks
Early months can bring more flares while crystal stores dissolve — the clinic can cover this period; it is not a reason to stop
Any rash on allopurinol is reported the same day — rare skin reactions are serious
Note flare triggers (a braai weekend, dehydration, a new diuretic) and tell the clinic — patterns change the plan
whenToSeekUrgentCare: A hot, red, swollen joint with fever — possible joint infection, which needs same-day care
A rash or mouth ulcers while on allopurinol
Flares that will not settle or that involve several joints at once
Very little urine passed, or kidney-area pain (urate can also form kidney stones)

source.authority: WHO / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

title: Heart Failure
about: A heart that cannot pump strongly enough — treated with daily medicines that take load off the heart, and daily watching of weight and breathlessness.
managementGoals: Medicines every day exactly as prescribed — they work together, and each protects differently
Daily weight, same time, same clothes: a gain of more than 2kg over three days means fluid is building and the clinic needs to know
Salt under one teaspoon a day; fluid only as the clinic has advised
Daily activity within comfort — walking to tolerance maintains fitness; rest between
Flu and pneumococcal vaccination yearly where the clinic advises
adherenceTips: Water tablets in the morning; a second dose, if prescribed, no later than early afternoon so sleep is possible
A weight-and-symptom diary brought to every visit changes the quality of care
Never stop tablets because the ankles are down and breathing easy — the medicines are why
Arrange pill collection through the chronic medicine system so standing in a queue never becomes the reason for running out
whenToSeekUrgentCare: Breathlessness at rest, or needing three pillows and still waking gasping
Weight gain over 2kg in three days, or rapid swelling of legs and tummy
Chest pain, fainting, or a suddenly irregular fast pulse
Coughing pink, frothy sputum — call 10177

source.authority: WHO / SA NDoH heart failure guidance

title: Chronic Hepatitis B
about: A lifelong liver infection, common in South Africa, that quietly inflames the liver over decades — monitored and, where active, treated with a daily tablet.
managementGoals: Regular monitoring as the clinic schedules — blood tests and a liver ultrasound about every six months watch for liver damage and liver cancer, which is the point of the whole follow-up
Where treatment is started (usually tenofovir-based), the tablet is taken daily without interruption, as with HIV treatment
Zero alcohol — alcohol and hepatitis B damage the same organ and multiply each other's harm
Vaccination of household members and sexual partners, and testing of children
Co-infection checks: HIV and hepatitis B are often found together and are treated together
adherenceTips: Attendance at monitoring visits matters even without symptoms — liver cancer caught small is treatable, caught late is not
Tell every clinician about the diagnosis before new medicines — the liver processes most medicines
Never share razors, toothbrushes or needles; cover cuts; use condoms
Keep hepatitis B medicine separate from antacid and iron doses by two hours (where tenofovir-based combination treatment applies)
whenToSeekUrgentCare: Yellow eyes, dark urine or pale stools with new tiredness
Vomiting blood or black tarry stools
Swollen tummy with leg swelling, or confusion in a person known to have cirrhosis
New right-upper tummy pain or a lump

source.authority: WHO hepatitis B guidance / SA NDoH
